story: The Atlas study from 2017 asked what the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, does for mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The authors showed that a lysosomal membrane protein called SLC38A9 senses the amino acid arginine and pushes essential amino acids such as leucine out of the lysosome. That leucine then helps switch mTORC1 on. The work used human cells and mice, and pancreatic cancer cells that live on protein they take in from outside needed SLC38A9 to form tumors.

Walter W. Chen is a middle author on this paper. PubMed lists him at the Whitehead Institute, MIT, the Koch Institute and the Broad Institute in Cambridge, and in the Harvard Medical School M.D.-Ph.D. Program. A Whitehead news item describes him as a graduate student in David Sabatini's lab who later became a pediatrics resident, and a UT Southwestern page lists a PhD from MIT in 2016, Harvard Medical School in 2018, pediatrics residency at Boston Children's Hospital in 2021 and a neonatal-perinatal fellowship at UT Southwestern in 2024. The same page gives his current title as Instructor in Pediatrics. His PubMed record also shows several other papers from the Sabatini group on cancer and mitochondrial metabolism.
